topic: Damaging Effects of Circulatory Arrest During Hypothermia
stem: Regarding the damaging effects of circulatory arrest during hypothermia, which statement about the **relative tolerance of organs** is correct?

choices.text: The brain's safe time is shortest, yet the kidney is sometimes damaged alone
The kidney has the shortest safe arrest time, and the brain is damaged only after the kidney
The spinal cord is more susceptible to ischemic injury than the brain is
At any temperature, the liver has a shorter safe arrest time than the kidney
Organs other than the brain are not damaged even by long periods of arrest

explanation.text: The ==brain== has the **shortest safe circulatory arrest time** of any organ or region, although the **kidney** occasionally seems to be damaged when the brain is not.

head: Organ
Tolerance of circulatory arrest (source)
rows: Shortest safe arrest time of any organ or region
Less susceptible to ischemic injury than the brain
Safe time longer than the brain's, shorter than the liver's (at any temperature)
60 min of arrest at 20°C–22°C: no structural or functional abnormality
explanation.caption: Organs and circulatory arrest

explanation.text: "Longer safe time" does not mean "immune": other organs **can be severely damaged** by long periods of arrest.
It is generally agreed that the brain has the shortest safe circulatory arrest time of any organ or region of the body
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 34

choiceNotes.b: It is generally agreed that the **brain** has the shortest safe arrest time; the kidney is only **occasionally** damaged when the brain is not.
choiceNotes.c: The spinal cord is **less** susceptible to ischemic injury than the brain (no deficits after arrest intervals of up to 60 minutes).
choiceNotes.d: At any temperature, the safe arrest time for the kidney is **shorter** than for the liver (and longer than for the brain).
choiceNotes.e: Other organs **can be severely damaged** by long periods of circulatory arrest; their safe arrest times are simply longer than the brain's.

stem: A neonate sustains brain injury in the setting of hypothermic circulatory arrest. How is this damage **most likely** to manifest, and what explanation does the source propose?

choices.text: Diffuse global injury, because all neonatal neurons are uniformly vulnerable to ischemia
Specific intellectual deficits, because cortical receptor density peaks in the neonatal period
Paraplegia, because the neonatal spinal cord is the region most sensitive to ischemia
Focal motor deficits, because receptor density in the motor cortex is highest at birth
Seizures or choreoathetosis, linked to high neonatal receptor density in the basal ganglia

explanation.text: In neonates, infants and small children, brain damage with circulatory arrest is more likely to show as ==seizures or choreoathetoid movements==; in adults, as **specific intellectual or motor deficits**.

steps.text: Density of specific membrane receptors varies with **age**
Receptors **transiently high in the basal ganglia** in the neonatal period
steps.label: neonate

steps.text: **Selective neuronal vulnerability** of these neuron groups
**Choreoathetosis** after ischemic injury in the very young
steps.label: ischemia

explanation.title: Definition
explanation.text: **Selective neuronal vulnerability** = a heightened sensitivity of specific neuron groups to ischemic injury.

Concentration of these receptors is transiently high in the basal ganglia in the neonatal period, which may relate to the appearance of choreoathetosis as a result of ischemic injury in the very young.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 34

choiceNotes.a: Brain damage with hypothermic circulatory arrest is **rarely diffuse**; the source invokes **selective** neuronal vulnerability of specific neuron groups.
choiceNotes.b: Specific intellectual or motor deficits are the usual pattern in **adults**; the receptor concentration that is transiently high in neonates is in the **basal ganglia**.
choiceNotes.c: The spinal cord is **less** susceptible than the brain; no trunk or limb deficits occur after arrest intervals of up to 60 minutes in infants.
choiceNotes.d: Focal (specific motor) deficits are the **adult** pattern; the source does not describe a neonatal peak of receptors in the motor cortex.

stem: While cooling a patient for planned hypothermic circulatory arrest, the team wants the temperature that best reflects **mean brain temperature**. Which monitoring sites should be used whenever possible?

choices.text: Tympanic membrane and nasopharynx
Rectum and bladder
Midesophagus and rectum
Extremity skin and bladder
Midesophagus and extremity skin

explanation.text: Temperature of the ==tympanic membrane and nasopharynx== most closely resembles **mean brain temperature**, so these sites should be used whenever possible.
Most clinical studies of temperature and safe arrest time are **flawed** by lack of information on the temperature of the brain itself and by the **variety of measurement sites** used.

Reflects mean brain temperature?
rows: Little consistent correlation between some sites

temperature of the tympanic membrane and nasopharynx most closely resembles mean temperature of the brain

stem: During a 30-minute period of circulatory arrest with the brain cooled to 15°C–20°C, what happens to **brain ATP** concentration?

choices.text: It falls to 20% of control values, signaling impending cell death
It falls to 35% of initial values and recovers rapidly on reperfusion
It remains unchanged, because cerebral metabolism is fully suppressed
It declines and then fails to recover in about half of the subjects
It declines to 35% and keeps falling during early reperfusion

explanation.text: With the brain at 15°C–20°C, ATP falls to ==35% of initial values== during 30 minutes of arrest but **returns rapidly to normal** during reperfusion.

head: Arrest with brain at 15°C–20°C
What the source reports
rows: Tolerated without evident structural or functional damage; ATP 35% -> rapid recovery
Associated with irreversible structural or functional damage; after 60 min, ATP **did not recover** in 2 of 4 animals (experimental)
explanation.caption: Temperature and duration

explanation.text: Do not confuse with the **kidney**: a rapid fall of ATP to **20%** of control indicates impending renal cell death in normothermic renal ischemia.
During such a period, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) concentrations decline to 35% of initial values but return rapidly to normal during reperfusion.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 34

choiceNotes.a: A rapid fall of ATP to 20% of control values is the indicator of impending **renal** cell death in normothermic kidney ischemia, not this brain finding.
choiceNotes.c: ATP does **decline**, to 35% of initial values, during such a period.
choiceNotes.d: Failure of ATP recovery in half (2 of 4) of animals was seen after **60 minutes** of hypothermic arrest, not 30.
choiceNotes.e: After 30 minutes at 15°C–20°C, ATP **returns rapidly to normal** during reperfusion.

stem: In experimental studies, histologic evidence of anoxic brain damage was found in **all** animals after 45–60 minutes of hypothermic circulatory arrest, yet some survived without evident functional abnormality. According to the source, which is the **most sensitive indicator** that an arrest period was not completely safe?

choices.text: An evident postoperative functional neurologic deficit
Failure to reach electrocerebral silence on EEG before the arrest
Histologic CNS changes, even without functional abnormality
Postoperative renal failure requiring dialysis
Abnormal postoperative liver function tests

explanation.text: ==Histologic changes in the central nervous system==, without functional abnormalities, are the **most sensitive indicators** of lack of complete safety of an arrest period.

head: Indicator of damage
Sensitivity
rows: Less sensitive: may be absent despite histologic damage

explanation.text: In experimental studies, histologic anoxic brain damage was found in **all** animals after 45–60 minutes of hypothermic arrest, although some survived **without evident functional abnormality**.

explanation.text: Fig. 2.9 defines "safe" arrest as the **absence of structural or functional damage**, so survival without a deficit does not prove the arrest was harmless.
histologic changes in the central nervous system, without functional abnormalities, are the most sensitive indicators of lack of complete safety of the arrest period used

choiceNotes.d: The kidney's safe arrest time is longer than the brain's, and postoperative renal failure is mainly attributed to low cardiac output and CPB effects.
choiceNotes.e: The liver tolerates arrest longer than the kidney or brain (60 minutes at 20°C–22°C causes no abnormality).

stem: In 394 patients undergoing aortic arch replacement with hypothermic circulatory arrest as the **sole means of brain preservation**, the stroke rate was about 13% in patients whose arrest exceeded a certain duration, versus 3.3% with shorter arrests. What was that duration?

choices.text: 20 minutes
30 minutes
50 minutes
60 minutes
40 minutes

explanation.text: Strokes occurred in ==13% (8 of 61)== when hypothermic circulatory arrest exceeded **40 minutes**, versus **3.3% (10 of 333)** with shorter arrest intervals.

head: Arrest duration
Strokes
Rate
explanation.caption: Aortic arch replacement, circulatory arrest alone

explanation.title: The source's summary
explanation.text: Intervals of hypothermic circulatory arrest of **40 minutes or more** are associated with brain injury in **infants, children, and adults**.

Some clinical series (e.g., arrest of 14–109 minutes at a mean nasopharyngeal temperature of 16.9°C) found no clinical brain damage attributed to arrest, but **comprehensive neuropsychometric studies were not undertaken**.
In summary, there is increasing evidence that intervals of hypothermic circulatory arrest of 40 minutes or more are associated with brain injury in infants, children, and adults.

choiceNotes.b: 30 minutes is the arrest tolerated without evident damage with the brain at 15°C–20°C; the stroke cut point in this series was **40 minutes**.
choiceNotes.c: Arrest over 50 minutes was a risk factor for delirium after pulmonary thromboendarterectomy; the stroke cut point here was **40 minutes**.
choiceNotes.d: Above 60 minutes, the prevalence of **temporary** neurologic dysfunction rises substantially; the stroke cut point here was **40 minutes**.

stem: A 70-year-old man has postoperative confusion, agitation and transient parkinsonism **without localizing signs** after ascending aorta and arch replacement with 65 minutes of hypothermic circulatory arrest. The symptoms resolve before discharge. Which statement about this complication is correct?

choices.text: Arrest duration and increasing age are incremental risk factors for it
It is uncommon, occurring in fewer than 2% of survivors
Its prevalence is similar with arrest shorter or longer than 60 minutes
It has no long-term significance once it has resolved
It is unrelated to arrest duration in pulmonary thromboendarterectomy

explanation.text: This is ==temporary neurologic dysfunction (TND)==; its incremental risk factors are **duration of hypothermic circulatory arrest** and **increasing patient age**.

children: Up to **20%** of survivors of thoracic aortic operations with arrest

explanation.text: "Temporary" does not mean "harmless": TND is a marker for long-term functional neurologic deficit.
Incremental risk factors associated with developing this complication are duration of hypothermic circulatory arrest and increasing patient age.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 35

choiceNotes.b: Temporary neurologic dysfunction can occur in **up to 20%** of survivors of thoracic aortic operations using hypothermic circulatory arrest.
choiceNotes.c: Its prevalence **increases substantially** when the arrest exceeds 60 minutes (Fig. 2.2).
choiceNotes.d: TND is a **marker for long-term functional neurologic deficit**; although not permanent, it can be an important complication.
choiceNotes.e: In pulmonary thromboendarterectomy, arrest times **over 50 minutes** were a powerful risk factor for postoperative delirium.

stem: Neurologic complications of aortic arch surgery are categorized as permanent (PND) or temporary (TND) neurologic dysfunction. Which definition matches the source?

choices.text: PND: confusion or delirium that resolves before discharge, with a normal brain CT
TND: a focal embolic stroke with a corresponding CT defect that improves before discharge
PND: a focal or global deficit with corresponding CT defects that persist at hospital discharge
TND: a global deficit (coma) with corresponding CT defects persisting at discharge
PND: any deficit present on the first postoperative day, whatever the CT findings

explanation.text: ==PND== = a **focal** (embolic stroke) or **global** (coma) deficit with corresponding **CT defects persisting at discharge**; ==TND== = non-focal dysfunction that **resolves before discharge** with a usually normal CT.

TND

explanation.title: P vs T
explanation.text: **P**ND = **P**ersists at discharge with **P**ictures (CT defects); **T**ND = **T**ransient, CT clean.
PND is defined as either a focal (embolic stroke) or global (coma) deficit with corresponding defects on CT scans that persist at discharge from the hospital.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 39

choiceNotes.b: TND is a **non-focal** neurocognitive dysfunction, and CT scans are usually **normal**.
choiceNotes.d: A global deficit (coma) with persisting CT defects is **PND**.
choiceNotes.e: PND requires a focal or global deficit with **corresponding CT defects** that **persist at discharge**.

stem: In dogs undergoing 30 minutes of hypothermic circulatory arrest, brain damage was seen when cooling on CPB used perfusate **20°C colder** than the animal, but was believed not to occur when the blood was only **4°C–6°C colder**. Which explanation does the source suggest?

choices.text: The cold perfusate directly triggered glutamate release
Short cooling with very cold blood caused uneven brain cooling
Cerebral blood flow was reduced during rewarming
High tissue glucose caused excessive glycolysis during arrest
The very cold blood lengthened the total cooling time

explanation.text: The damage was probably related to the ==short cooling period== with very cold blood, which produced **uneven brain cooling**.

explanation.title: Principle
explanation.text: **Uneven cooling of the brain** is probably a risk factor for brain damage, although the evidence is largely indirect.
The longer period of cooling required with the blood only 4°C to 6°C colder than the subject probably produced more uniform cooling.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 35

choiceNotes.a: Glutamate excitotoxicity is described under the biochemical milieu with energy depletion; it is not the source's explanation for this finding.
choiceNotes.c: Reduced flow during rewarming is a separate observation; the source attributes this finding to **uneven cooling** from a short cooling period.
choiceNotes.d: Glucose-driven lactic acidosis is a separate biochemical risk; it is not the explanation offered here.
choiceNotes.e: The opposite: very cold blood required a **short** cooling period; the 4°C–6°C gradient required the **longer** one.

stem: In 218 young patients undergoing repair of VSD, tetralogy of Fallot, transposition or AV septal defect with hypothermic circulatory arrest (mean arrest about 42 minutes, mean temperature 19.7°C in both groups), how did the **cooling method** relate to major neurologic events?

choices.text: Events occurred only after surface cooling to 28°C followed by core cooling
Event rates were similar, because arrest time and temperature were matched
Core cooling alone was safer, because it shortened the time before arrest
The excess events after core cooling reflected longer arrest times in that group
Events occurred only after core cooling alone, not after surface cooling first

explanation.text: Major neurologic events occurred in ==6% with core cooling by CPB alone== and in **0%** with **surface cooling to 28°C followed by core cooling**.

items: In neonates and infants, **rapid** core cooling was associated with more neurologic deficits than **more prolonged** core cooling.
In this series, **no** major event occurred when arrest lasted **less than 45 minutes**; the probability rose as arrest time increased beyond this (Fig. 2.6).

explanation.text: Table 2.2 **excludes seizures** followed by uneventful convalescence from major neurologic events.
A reasonable presumption is that the more rapid core cooling resulted in uneven cooling of the brain.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 35

choiceNotes.a: The reverse: surface cooling to 28°C then core cooling had **0** major events; core cooling alone had **8 (6%)**.
choiceNotes.b: Despite similar arrest times and temperatures, the rates differed: 0% vs 6% (P = .03).
choiceNotes.c: Core cooling alone had **more** events; the presumption is that more rapid core cooling caused **uneven** brain cooling.
choiceNotes.d: Mean arrest times were essentially equal: 42.5 minutes (surface then core) vs 42.8 minutes (core only).

stem: Cerebral blood flow and metabolism are measured in children during cooling before hypothermic circulatory arrest. Which **pre-arrest** finding suggests particular vulnerability to cerebral injury?

choices.text: A parallel fall in cerebral blood flow and cerebral oxygen consumption
Preserved flow–metabolism coupling at low temperature under alpha-stat
Electrocerebral silence on EEG for 3 minutes before the arrest
Low arterial pressure during CPB, now firmly established as causal
Increased cerebral oxygen extraction before the circulatory arrest

explanation.text: Children with ==increased oxygen extraction before circulatory arrest== may be particularly vulnerable to cerebral injury: flow was probably **inadequate for metabolic requirements**.

steps.text: **Cooling**: cerebral blood flow and O~2~ consumption fall **in parallel**
Cerebral blood flow probably **inadequate** for metabolic requirements

explanation.text: In **3 of 4** patients later found to have neurologic injury, oxygen extraction before the arrest was **increased**.

explanation.text: Cerebral blood flow generally decreases with temperature during cooling, and coupling with metabolism is maintained even at low temperatures under the **alpha-stat** strategy.
patients with increased oxygen extraction before circulatory arrest may be particularly vulnerable to cerebral injury

choiceNotes.b: Coupling maintained at low temperatures with alpha-stat management was the usual finding, not a marker of vulnerability.
choiceNotes.c: Electrocerebral silence before arrest accompanied the **longest** recorded safe arrests in adults.
choiceNotes.d: The role of hypotension during CPB in neurologic dysfunction **now appears less certain**.

stem: Which statement about **cerebral blood flow during rewarming** after hypothermic circulatory arrest is correct?

choices.text: It is reduced, yet jugular saturation suggests adequate O~2~ delivery in infants
It rises above baseline, producing hyperemia as soon as rewarming starts
It is reduced in experimental animals but not in humans
It is reduced only after circulatory arrest, never with continuous CPB
It is reduced, and jugular venous saturation shows inadequate oxygen delivery

explanation.text: Cerebral blood flow is ==reduced during rewarming== after circulatory arrest; in infants, **jugular venous oxygen saturation** suggests oxygen delivery is still **adequate**.

items: **Experimental**: flow is reduced during rewarming after arrest (Fig. 2.3).
**Humans**: occurs during cardiac surgery **with or without** arrest, and may affect outcomes.
**Infants**: reduced immediately after arrest **and** after achieving normothermia.

explanation.title: Fig. 2.3
explanation.text: In gerbils, flow during rewarming was **lower** after 48 minutes of total cessation of cerebral blood flow at 18°C than after continued hypothermic perfusion.
In infants, cerebral blood flow is reduced during rewarming immediately after hypothermic circulatory arrest and after achieving normothermia.

choiceNotes.b: Experimental and clinical studies show cerebral blood flow is **reduced**, not increased, during rewarming after arrest.
choiceNotes.c: The phenomenon **occurs in humans** during cardiac surgery and may affect outcomes.
choiceNotes.d: It occurs in humans **with or without** circulatory arrest.
choiceNotes.e: In infants, based on jugular venous oxygen saturation, oxygen delivery **appears adequate** during this period of reduced flow.

stem: Before neonatal repair with planned hypothermic circulatory arrest, the perfusionist proposes a **glucose-containing pump prime**. Which response is supported by the source?

choices.text: Use glucose, because it keeps brain ATP normal throughout a long arrest
Glucose is acceptable, because the biochemical milieu does not affect outcome
Avoid glucose only because it raises cerebral blood flow during cooling
Avoid glucose in prime and IV fluids: risk of excess glycolysis and lactic acid
Use glucose, because tissue glucose is usually low when arrest begins

explanation.text: It is ==imprudent to use glucose solutions== for the prime or IV infusion when circulatory arrest is planned: **increased tissue glucose** may cause **lactic acid** injury during the arrest.

steps.text: **Increased tissue glucose** at the start of arrest (usual)

explanation.title: Practical rule
explanation.text: No glucose in the **pump-oxygenator prime** and no glucose **IV infusion** when a period of circulatory arrest is contemplated.
Arterial **pH and PCO~2~** during cooling may affect brain tissue directly or via cerebral blood flow, but any effect on neurologic outcome is **uncertain**.
This possibility makes it imprudent to use glucose solutions for priming the pump-oxygenator and for intravenous infusion when a period of circulatory arrest is contemplated.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 36

choiceNotes.a: Brain ATP declines during arrest; increased tissue glucose may instead lead to excessive glycolysis and **lactic acid** accumulation.
choiceNotes.b: The biochemical milieu is listed among risk factors for brain damage; the glucose concern makes its use **imprudent**.
choiceNotes.c: The source's reason is excessive glycolysis and acidosis during the arrest, not cerebral blood flow.
choiceNotes.e: Increased tissue glucose is **usually present** at the beginning of the arrest period.

stem: Which sequence best describes how **glutamate** contributes to neuronal injury during cellular energy depletion, such as cerebral ischemia during circulatory arrest?

choices.text: Excess reuptake -> glutamate depletion -> loss of excitation -> intracellular calcium falls -> cell death
Failed reuptake -> glutamate excess -> receptor blockade -> intracellular calcium falls -> cell death
Excess glycolysis -> glutamate synthesis -> lactic acid rises -> intracellular calcium falls -> cell death
Failed reuptake -> glutamate excess -> receptor overexcitation -> intracellular calcium rises -> cell death
Failed reuptake -> glutamate excess -> receptor overexcitation -> calcium rises -> apoptosis only

explanation.text: When energy is depleted, the **energy-dependent synaptic reuptake** of glutamate fails; ==glutamate accumulates==, overexcites its receptors, **intracellular calcium rises**, and neurons are injured and die.

steps.text: Neuronal injury and death (**necrosis and apoptosis**)

explanation.text: **Glutamate** is the major transmitter mediating synaptic excitation in the mammalian central nervous system; this process was seen in experimental animals after **2 hours** of circulatory arrest.
Resulting overaccumulation of glutamate leads to excessive excitation of the glutamate receptors, leading to an increase in intracellular calcium and eventual neuronal cell injury and death.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 36

choiceNotes.a: Synaptic reuptake is energy dependent and is **compromised**, so glutamate **accumulates**; it is not depleted.
choiceNotes.b: Excess glutamate causes **excessive excitation** of its receptors and a **rise** in intracellular calcium.
choiceNotes.c: Glycolysis and lactic acid relate to increased tissue glucose, a separate mechanism; calcium **rises** in excitotoxicity.
choiceNotes.e: Glutamate excitotoxicity after hypothermic arrest mediates neuronal **apoptosis as well as necrosis**.

stem: Neuronal necrosis after prolonged circulatory arrest is **selective**. Which brain regions are characteristically **most vulnerable** to excitatory amino acid injury?

choices.text: Superficial neocortex, brainstem and spinal cord
Hippocampus, cerebellum and basal ganglia
Frontal white matter, thalamus and pons
Neocortex alone, sparing deeper structures
Spinal cord gray matter and brainstem nuclei

explanation.text: The ==hippocampus, cerebellum and basal ganglia==, rich in **glutamate receptors**, are characteristically most vulnerable, implying **excitation** as an underlying mechanism.
Neuronal necrosis is **selective** and corresponds closely to the **distribution of excitatory amino acid receptors**.

children: Most vulnerable area to prolonged (> 70 min) arrest at 15°C (experimental histopathology)
Receptors transiently high in neonates -> choreoathetosis

explanation.text: The hippocampus, cerebellum, and basal ganglia, which have high concentrations of glutamate receptors, are characteristically most vulnerable to this injury, implying excitation as an underlying mechanism.
